This supervision and remote interaction from an operational control center is described by the SAE Automated Vehicle Safety Consortium as “remote assistance.” Within an operational control center, personnel also provide a human interface with passengers by responding to passenger inquiries via intercom or video links within stations and in vehicles. 4.2.2 ASDC Benefits for Automation of ODT Services NLR studies of conventional ODT service using human operators revealed practical limitations of how the vehicle fleet can be dispatched to respond to ridership surge flows. Such capacity limitations commonly occur when the ridership surge conditions result from the following: • Random peaking effects within the pattern of origin/destination trips • Scheduled event patterns that concentrate person-trips at certain times of day (e.g., campus class schedules, medical complex appointment schedules, sporting events) • Arrival of large regional transit and/or intercity trains at intermodal stations within the AMD network when all or most passengers are boarding the ODT system for FMLM connections. For a conventional ODT system, capacity limitations arise primarily from personnel management. The result is that conventional ODT cannot support a fleet size needed to serve peak surge demands because it would result in many vehicles (and their associated drivers) being 44 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. dormant during the extended periods of the day with off-peak demand conditions. Commercial ride-hailing services address surge demand with surge pricing, in which escalated prices for riders encourage riders to seek off-peak periods. Escalated pay for drivers also encourages more drivers to come online during peak periods. However, ODT, as currently implemented, does not leverage market forces such as surge pricing to help balance supply and demand. As a result of these practical limitations, ODT passengers typically experience degraded service equating to extensive delay during periods of peak demand or even being notified that no operator/vehicle is available at that time, with an advisement that they should try again later. However, AV fleets under an ASDC subsystem can bring additional flexibility to better respond to peak demand. AV fleets can more aptly increase or decrease fleet size in response to trip demand without penalties for dormant vehicles and operators. Further, the ASDC can more aptly deploy larger vehicles to the dominant station pairs to better serve demand while reserving smaller vehicles to station pairs with less demand. Further, the ASDC can optimally manage a fleet by placing the required “surplus” vehicles in storage areas located at strategic points near the known places where ridership demand-surge flows will occur. Converting the operating fleet to AV technology and replacing the conventional dispatching procedures/system with a fully automated supervisory and dispatch control system allows most capacity deficiencies because of fleet size limitations to be effectively addressed. 4.3 BEV Fleet Charging Strategy and Infrastructure The convergence of vehicle electrification with the automation of vehicle fleets adds to the challenges of planning for AMD fleet operations.
